questions.q: How many pieces of information can the brain juggle at once, according to the summary?
a: Three to five
One or two
Seven to nine
Ten to twelve
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the mind can hold only three to five items at a time, which is why structured chunks are easier to remember.

questions.q: What do studies say about people who suffer from excessive inner chatter?
a: They listen poorly and overshare, which pushes friends away
They become unusually calm in social situations
They remember far more of what they read
They seek out more contact with strangers
questions.why: The summary notes that heavy chatter makes people poor listeners who do not know when to stop oversharing.

questions.q: What does the author suggest doing when a problem feels overwhelming?
a: Zoom out and view it from another perspective or time
Replay the problem until its cause becomes clear
Distract yourself with work until the feeling fades
Push the thought away whenever it appears
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends stepping back, imagining a friend's problem, or asking how much it will matter later.

questions.q: What is temporal distancing, as described in the summary?
a: Asking how much the problem will matter years from now
Imagining the problem happened to a close friend
Writing about the problem every morning
Breaking the problem into smaller tasks
questions.why: The summary defines temporal distancing as thinking about how little a current problem will matter in ten years or another long span.

questions.q: Why isn't talking about your pain enough to move past it?
a: We also need fresh perspective, not just empathy
We need to suppress the memory completely
We should avoid discussing painful events at all
Only trained professionals can make us feel heard
questions.why: Lesson 3 says our brain needs to heal as well as our heart, so we need people who offer solutions and new viewpoints.
